In [[polyhedral combinatorics]], the '''hypersimplex''' <math>\Delta_{d,k}</math> is a [[convex polytope]] that generalizes the [[simplex]]. It is determined by two integers <math>d</math> and <math>k</math>, and is defined as the [[convex hull]] of the <math>d</math>-dimensional [[vector (mathematics)|vectors]] whose coefficients consist of <math>k</math> ones and <math>d-k</math> zeros. Equivalently, <math>\Delta_{d,k}</math> can be obtained by slicing the <math>d</math>-dimensional unit [[hypercube]] <math>[0,1]^d</math> with the [[hyperplane]] of equation <math>x_1+\cdots+x_d=k</math> and, for this reason, it is a <math>(d-1)</math>-dimensional polytope when <math>0<k<d</math>.<ref name="gc">{{citation|title=Geometric Combinatorics|volume=13|series=IAS/Park City mathematics series|first1=Ezra|last1=Miller|first2=Victor|last2=Reiner|first3=Bernd|last3=Sturmfels|author3-link=Bernd Sturmfels|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=9780821886953|page=655|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=W_SPdwfPTw8C&pg=PA655}}.</ref>

==Properties==
The number of vertices of <math>\Delta_{d,k}</math> is <math>\tbinom d k </math>.<ref name="gc"/> The [[Graph of a polytope|vertex-edge graph]] of the hypersimplex <math>\Delta_{d,k}</math> is the [[Johnson graph]] <math>J(d,k)</math>.<ref>{{citation|first=Fred J.|last=Rispoli|title=The graph of the hypersimplex|year=2008|arxiv=0811.2981|bibcode=2008arXiv0811.2981R}}.</ref>

==Alternative constructions==
An alternative construction (for <math>0 < k < d</math>) is to take the convex hull of all <math>(d-1)</math>-dimensional <math>(0,1)</math>-vectors that have either <math>k-1</math> or <math>k</math> nonzero coordinates. This has the advantage of operating in a space that is the same dimension as the resulting polytope, but the disadvantage that the polytope it produces is less symmetric (although combinatorially equivalent to the result of the other construction).

The hypersimplex <math>\Delta_{d,k}</math> is also the [[matroid polytope]] for a [[uniform matroid]] with <math>d</math> elements and rank <math>k</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Grötschel | first = Martin | author-link = Martin Grötschel
 | contribution = Cardinality homogeneous set systems, cycles in matroids, and associated polytopes
 | mr = 2077557
 | pages = 99–120
 | publisher = SIAM, Philadelphia, PA
 | series = MPS/SIAM Ser. Optim.
 | title = The Sharpest Cut: The Impact of Manfred Padberg and His Work
 | year = 2004}}. See in particular the remarks following Prop.&nbsp;8.20 on [https://books.google.com/books?id=iXJxerJLyTEC&oi=fnd&pg=PA114 p.&nbsp;114].</ref>

== Examples==
The hypersimplex <math>\Delta_{d,1}</math> is a <math>(d-1)</math>-simplex (and therefore, it has <math>d</math> vertices).
The hypersimplex <math>\Delta_{4,2}</math> is an [[octahedron]], and the hypersimplex <math>\Delta_{5,2}</math> is a [[rectified 5-cell]].

Generally, the hypersimplex, <math>\Delta_{d,k}</math>, corresponds to a [[uniform polytope]], being the <math>(k-1)</math>-[[Rectification (geometry)|rectified]] <math>(d-1)</math>-dimensional simplex, with vertices positioned at the center of all the <math>(k-1)</math>-dimensional faces of a <math>(d-1)</math>-dimensional simplex.

==History==
The hypersimplices were first studied and named in the computation of [[characteristic class]]es (an important topic in [[algebraic topology]]), by {{harvtxt|Gabrièlov|Gelʹfand|Losik|1975}}.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Gabrièlov | first1 = A. M.
